big: A fund can hold shares, yet barely move when the share market does. That sounds like a trick. It is not, and the idea behind it is called arbitrage.

lines: I have ₹20 lakh lying idle for a year. Anything safer than equity but better taxed than an FD?
There is a fund for this, but the way it earns is unusual. Watch one share first, then the tax.

h: One share, two very different months
alt: Two sets of bars showing a hedged share when the price falls and when it rises, with the same locked profit
caps: The fund buys a share at ₹1,000 in the cash market. It sells the same share in futures at ₹1,005.
Case 1: the share falls to ₹900. The cash share loses ₹100. The futures sale gains ₹105.
Case 2: the share rises to ₹1,100. The share gains ₹100. The futures sale loses ₹95.
Either way the fund is left with the ₹5 gap it locked in. That is arbitrage.

rows: Tax as a share of the gain (%)
alt: Two sets of bars comparing a fixed deposit and an arbitrage fund after tax for someone in the 30 percent slab
caps: Assume ₹20 lakh for a year. The FD pays 7%. The arbitrage fund returns 6.5%. Both are assumptions.
FD interest is taxed at the 30% slab plus 4% cess (31.2%), so ₹43,680 goes in tax.
Redeemed at 12 months, the arbitrage gain is taxed at 20% plus cess (20.8%): ₹27,040.
The lower return leaves more in hand: ₹1,02,960 against ₹96,320. Rates here are assumed.

title: Fair claims, and unfair ones
stops: Moves little with the stock market
Can dip when futures premiums shrink
alt: A shield with true and false statements about arbitrage funds
caps: It is hedged, so it barely moves when the stock market falls, and it is taxed as an equity fund.
Its returns follow short-term rates and can dip when the futures premium narrows.
It is a parking place for money, not a way to grow wealth over many years.

q: An arbitrage fund buys a share at ₹1,000 and sells its futures at ₹1,005. By month end the share has fallen to ₹950 and the futures price has merged with it. What does the fund make on this share?
opts: ₹50 loss, as the share price fell and the fund owns that share
₹5 gain, as a ₹50 share loss is met by a ₹55 futures gain
₹55 gain, as the futures sale made money while the share fell
Nothing, because a hedged position never earns or loses a rupee
why: The hedge matters. The ₹50 fall on the share is offset by a profit on the futures sale it sold.
The share loses ₹50, the futures sale gains ₹55, and the locked gap of ₹5 remains.
The ₹55 futures gain is real, but the ₹50 share loss cancels most of it, leaving only ₹5.
The gap between the two prices is the profit, so a hedged position still earns that small sum.

q: Rohan is in the 30% slab and will redeem after 12 months. Which reply to his ₹20 lakh question is honest?
opts: It will certainly beat an FD, since equity tax is always lower
It is exempt from tax, since equity funds are taxed unlike income
It may leave more after tax than an FD, at similar returns
It will grow like equity over the year, with a hedge as a bonus
why: If the futures premium narrows, the return can fall below an FD's, so a sure win cannot be promised.
Equity taxation is not zero. Short-term gains at 12 months or less are taxed at 20% plus cess in the example.
It claims only what the example shows: a lower tax rate helps, while the return stays near short-term rates.
A hedged fund does not chase equity growth. Its return follows short-term rates, so this promise is wrong.

q: In a weak market, an arbitrage fund's returns slip from about 7% to about 5.5% a year. No stock it holds has crashed. What explains the dip?
opts: The hedge has failed, so the fund is now losing on its stocks
The fund has moved most of its money into small caps for returns
Rates always rise when equity falls, which cuts the fund's income
Cash and futures prices drew closer, so less gap is locked in
why: A hedge that has failed would cause sharp losses, not a slow slide. This fund just earns a thinner gap.
Arbitrage funds stay hedged and do not shift into small caps. Their earnings come from the price gap.
Rates and equity markets do not move in lockstep. The dip here comes from the shrinking futures premium.
The fund earns the gap between cash and futures prices. In weak markets demand for leverage falls and the gap shrinks.

q: A client wants to put money in an arbitrage fund for ten years, because it is taxed as equity. What should the adviser say?
opts: It is ideal, since equity taxation also brings equity-like returns
It suits parking cash, but a ten-year goal needs a growth fund
It works, as the futures gap grows larger each year it is held
It works only if she invests by SIP and never redeems early
why: Equity tax treatment is about tax rules, not returns. The fund still earns near short-term rates.
Returns track short-term rates, so over ten years it will trail the growth a long-term goal needs.
The gap between cash and futures is small and does not compound upward the longer the fund is held.
A SIP changes how money goes in, not what the fund earns. The return stays near short-term rates.

pts: Arbitrage funds buy in cash, sell in futures and lock in the gap.
They are hedged and taxed as equity, but they earn near short-term rates.
Use them to park money for about a year, not to grow it for a decade.
